notable_claims: System administrators are often unfairly targeted in discussions regarding computer access and restrictions.
User ignorance of system limits (e.g., excessive background jobs or print requests) creates significant administrative strain.
classification.summary: Wes Morgan defends system administrators against criticisms voiced in the discussion group. He argues that users often lack an understanding of the technical and logistical burdens placed on admins, such as managing resource-heavy jobs and user demands. The post encourages empathy for those managing shared computing resources to avoid blanket condemnations.
classification.title: Have you walked the proverbial mile?

identity.subject: Have you walked the proverbial mile?

notable_claims: Administrative power without due process can stunt a student's education by discouraging exploration beyond the curriculum.
There is a need for formal rules and rights to govern the relationship between system administrators and users.
classification.summary: Sean Casey argues for established rules and rights for both system administrators and users to prevent arbitrary exercises of power. He recounts a personal experience at the University of Kentucky where a professor used administrative privileges to search his files and discourage 'hacking' after he exceeded connect-time limits while writing shell scripts. The author highlights the 'chilling effect' such administration has on student curiosity and academic exploration.
classification.title: Re: Have you walked the proverbial mile?

identity.subject: Re: Have you walked the proverbial mile?

notable_claims: System administrators may target individual users to reduce their overall workload.
Sysadmins have used account suspensions and monitoring of user files as a means of control.
classification.summary: Matthew T. Russotto responds to a system administrator's claim that admins are too busy to persecute users. Russotto describes personal experiences of account suspension and surveillance by sysadmins on VAXstations. He argues that some administrators target specific 'troublemaker' users to reduce their own workload.
classification.title: Re: Have you walked the proverbial mile?

identity.subject: Re: Have you walked the proverbial mile?

notable_claims: Locking a student's account in an academic setting can be tantamount to expulsion.
System administrators should treat users as 'innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt'.
Good system administration should be as invisible as possible.
classification.summary: Charlie Martin shares a personal anecdote about a system administrator deleting his mail archives without notice to save disk space. He argues that system administrators in academic settings should exercise restraint and avoid locking accounts, as losing computer access can be equivalent to expulsion for students. The post emphasizes the need for due process and measured responses when dealing with user errors or antisocial behavior on shared systems.
classification.title: War story and some thoughts....

notable_claims: UIUC computer usage rules were rewritten as a result of the author's actions.
The CSO allegedly used bureaucratic delays to maintain an indefinite account suspension without due process.
classification.summary: Mike Neuliep describes how the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) Computing Services Office (CSO) suspended his accounts following a Usenet flame war with a CSO employee. Neuliep alleges that the CSO intentionally failed to file the case with the Student Disciplinary Committee to keep his accounts suspended indefinitely without a hearing. He claims this bureaucratic maneuver was used to punish 'maverick' users and led to the rewriting of university computer usage rules.
classification.title: My Punishment

notable_claims: The CS department would not have suspended accounts based solely on the CSO's request.
classification.summary: Paul Pomes of the University of Illinois CSO responds to a previous post regarding student punishments and account suspensions. He challenges the anonymity and specifics of a former student's claims about administrative actions taken by the CSO and the Computer Science department.
classification.title: Re: My Punishment

notable_claims: System administrators should have the power to suspend privileges to preserve order, but not to punish users.
Users are entitled to clear statements of policy and timely procedures for appeal regarding administrative actions.
The right to punish should be reserved for institutional authorities such as provosts or deans rather than system administrators.
classification.summary: William Hugh Murray proposes a framework for system administration policies to balance order with user rights. He argues that administrative suspensions should be used only to preserve system stability, not as punishment, and that formal disciplinary actions should be reserved for institutional authorities.
classification.title: Punishment

notable_claims: Some colleges previously blocked all student internet access due to a 'don't let them do anything' mentality.
System administrators face a conflict between inconveniencing one user and ensuring stability for the entire user base.
classification.summary: Miles Oursler, a systems manager at Kenyon College, contributes to a debate regarding the conduct of system administrators and student rights. He describes his efforts to overturn restrictive policies that previously blocked student internet access based on fear of misuse. The post discusses the tension between maintaining system stability for all users and the fair treatment of individual students who violate rules.
classification.title: Slime and Punishment

notable_claims: Users are often punished more severely for follow-up infractions than for the original offense.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides advice to computer users on how to handle disputes with system administrators. He warns that committing further rule infractions during a protest often leads to more severe punishments than the original offense. The post emphasizes the distinction between the right to appeal a rule and the right to violate it.
classification.title: How to back a user into a corner

identity.subject: Re: How to back a user into a corner

notable_claims: System abuse is primarily a result of poor communication between systems staff and users.
Explaining the reasons for system restrictions reduces user frustration and can lead to user support for those restrictions.
organizations: State University of New York, Stony Brook
classification.summary: Sanjay Kapur, a systems administrator at SUNY Stony Brook, discusses the importance of communication between technical staff and users. He argues that system abuse is typically caused by a lack of communication rather than malice. He advocates for direct access to systems staff as a central element of institutional policy to reduce user frustration.
classification.title: Users and Systems staff interaction

notable_claims: Accounts were suspended during Internet and DECnet worm outbreaks if usernames matched passwords.
Account suspensions are primarily triggered automatically by a lack of allocated funds.
Files are archived upon account deletion if requested by the user.
organizations: State University of New York, Stony Brook
classification.summary: Sanjay Kapur, a system administrator at SUNY Stony Brook, outlines the specific criteria used for suspending or deleting user accounts. He describes policies regarding funding exhaustion, security risks during worm outbreaks, and administrative deletions due to affiliation changes. The post seeks feedback on whether these standard administrative practices constitute 'wrongful' denials of service.
classification.title: Account suspensions and other denial of services in practice

identity.subject: Account suspensions and other denial of services in practice.

notable_claims: The term 'theft of service' is too broad to meet the standard of being clearly defined.
Vague computer policies can be used to categorize any violation as theft of service.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie argues that the term 'theft of service' is too vague to be used as a basis for disciplinary action against computer users. He contends that such broad terminology allows any policy violation to be categorized as theft, contradicting principles of clarity and reasonableness.
classification.title: User theft of service

notable_claims: The CAF discussions were hosted via eff.org
Discussion moved to alt.comp.acad-freedom.talk and alt.comp.acad-freedom.news
classification.summary: Carl Kadie announces that Computers and Academic Freedom discussions have expanded from mailing lists to Usenet newsgroups. He outlines the technical advantages of newsgroups, including better disk usage and reduced administrative overhead. The transition includes both an unmoderated 'talk' group and a moderated 'news' group.
classification.title: Switching from the mailing lists to the newsgroups

identity.subject: Switching from the mailing lists to the newsgroups
